title: Why Is My Dog Scratching So Much? Common Causes and What to Do
summary: A practical guide to common reasons dogs itch, what owners can safely check at home, and signs that warrant veterinary care.
primaryKeyword: why is my dog scratching so much
secondaryKeywords: when to see vet for dog itching
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog scratching its side while an owner gently checks the coat
content:
Frequent scratching is not something to ignore. An occasional scratch is normal, but repeated scratching, licking, chewing, rubbing, or skin damage can point to parasites, allergies, infection, pain, or another problem that needs attention. The safest approach is to look for patterns, protect the skin from further injury, and involve a veterinarian when itching is persistent or severe.

Common reasons dogs scratch

Itching is a symptom rather than a diagnosis. Fleas are one possible cause, but they are not the only one. Dogs may itch because of flea allergy, environmental allergies, food-related reactions, mites, bacterial or yeast skin infections, dry or irritated skin, contact with an irritant, or problems affecting the ears and paws.

1. Fleas and flea allergy

Some dogs react strongly to flea bites, so you may not see many fleas even when they are contributing to the problem. Check around the base of the tail, belly, groin, and inner thighs for fleas or dark debris. Ask your veterinarian which parasite prevention is appropriate for your dog rather than combining products on your own.

2. Environmental allergies

Pollen, grasses, molds, and dust-related allergens can contribute to recurring itch. Dogs with environmental allergy often lick or chew their paws, rub their face, develop repeated ear trouble, or become itchier during particular seasons. A calendar noting flare-ups can be useful when speaking with your veterinarian.

3. Skin infection

Persistent scratching can damage the skin barrier, and infection can make itching worse. Redness, odor, greasy skin, crusts, pustules, moist patches, or hair loss deserve veterinary assessment. Skin infections often need the underlying trigger addressed as well as the infection itself.

4. Ear or paw problems

A dog that scratches mainly around the ears, shakes the head, or has ear odor may have an ear problem. Repeated paw licking can accompany allergy, irritation, infection, a foreign object, or injury. Avoid inserting cotton swabs or unprescribed products into an irritated ear.

What you can safely do today

  • Look through the coat in good light for fleas, debris, redness, wounds, swelling, or hair loss.
  • Check paws and between the toes for cuts, thorns, swelling, or damaged nails.
  • Wash bedding and keep the dog's resting area clean.
  • Prevent excessive self-trauma while arranging care; your veterinarian can advise on a safe protective collar if needed.
  • Write down when the itching started, where it occurs, recent diet changes, parasite prevention, grooming products, and whether it is seasonal.

What not to do

Do not give human medicines, apply essential oils, use leftover antibiotics, or repeatedly change foods and shampoos without a plan. These steps can cause side effects or make the underlying problem harder to identify. A food trial for suspected food allergy is most useful when designed and monitored by a veterinarian.

When to contact a veterinarian

Arrange veterinary care if scratching lasts more than a few days, repeatedly returns, interrupts sleep, or causes hair loss, odor, scabs, ear discharge, or sore skin. Seek prompt care for facial swelling, breathing difficulty, rapidly spreading hives, severe pain, extensive wounds, marked lethargy, or other sudden systemic signs.

Track the pattern, not just the scratch

Where and when a dog itches can be useful information. Paw licking plus recurring ear irritation, for example, creates a different clinical picture from sudden scratching after outdoor exposure. Photos taken during flare-ups can also help if the skin looks better by the appointment.

Related Virixoo guides

If your dog is also licking the paws repeatedly, read Why Does My Dog Lick His Paws?. If the problem is focused on the ears, see Why Does My Dog Shake His Head?.

Trusted reference

For general veterinary guidance and preventive-care information, visit the American Animal Hospital Association (AAHA).

FAQ

Can a dog itch even if I cannot see fleas?

Yes. Fleas can be difficult to find, and some dogs are very sensitive to bites. Other causes such as allergy, mites, infection, and irritation are also possible.

Should I change my dog's food immediately?

Not automatically. Random diet changes can make assessment harder. If food allergy is suspected, ask your veterinarian about a controlled elimination diet.

Is constant paw licking a type of itching?

It can be. Licking and chewing are common ways dogs respond to itch, irritation, discomfort, or pain.

Bottom line: Persistent itching deserves a cause-focused approach. Check for obvious problems, prevent self-injury, document the pattern, and get veterinary help when signs persist or the skin becomes damaged.

title: Why Does My Dog Lick His Paws? 9 Possible Reasons and Safe Next Steps
summary: Paw licking can be normal grooming or a clue to allergy, irritation, injury, infection, or pain. Learn what to check and when to call your vet.
primaryKeyword: why does my dog lick his paws
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog gently licking a front paw while owner inspects it
content:
A few licks after a walk can be normal; repeated licking is different. If your dog keeps returning to one paw or spends long periods chewing several paws, look for a physical trigger before assuming it is simply a habit.

Why dogs lick their paws

1. Something is stuck or irritating the paw

Grass seeds, small thorns, road debris, salt, sand, or sticky material can irritate the pads or spaces between the toes. Compare all four paws and look for swelling, redness, cuts, or a foreign object that is sitting superficially. Do not dig into the skin to remove deeply embedded material.

2. A minor injury

Cracked pads, torn nails, abrasions, and insect stings can lead to sudden licking of one paw. Limping, guarding the foot, bleeding, or obvious pain increases the need for veterinary assessment.

3. Allergy or skin disease

Dogs with environmental allergies commonly develop itchy feet. Several paws may be affected, and ear or skin problems may occur at the same time. Food-related reactions are another possibility, but they cannot be diagnosed simply from paw licking.

4. Infection

Moisture and repeated licking can contribute to an unhealthy skin environment. Odor, discharge, marked redness, swelling, crusting, or sores should be evaluated by a veterinarian because bacterial or yeast overgrowth may require targeted treatment.

5. Pain away from the skin

Some dogs lick an area that hurts because of a joint, nail, toe, or other musculoskeletal problem. Persistent licking of one limb without obvious skin disease is still worth discussing with your veterinarian.

6. Stress or repetitive behavior

After medical causes have been considered, stress, boredom, or a repetitive behavior pattern may play a role. Increasing appropriate exercise, enrichment, predictable routines, and calm training can help, but compulsive licking should not be treated as purely behavioral until physical causes are addressed.

A simple paw check

  1. Choose a calm, well-lit area.
  2. Compare the paw with the opposite foot.
  3. Inspect the pads, nails, nail beds, and spaces between toes.
  4. Note heat, swelling, odor, moisture, redness, cuts, or discharge.
  5. Stop if your dog is painful or becomes defensive.

After walks

If your dog is sensitive to outdoor irritants, rinsing or wiping paws with plain water and drying them thoroughly may help remove surface debris. Avoid harsh cleaners or fragranced products unless your veterinarian recommends them.

When veterinary care is important

Contact a veterinarian for persistent licking, recurring redness, limping, swelling, broken nails, discharge, odor, bleeding, deep wounds, or significant pain. Sudden facial swelling, hives, breathing trouble, or collapse requires urgent veterinary attention.

Related Virixoo guides

For broader skin symptoms, see Why Is My Dog Scratching So Much?. If your dog also has repeated ear or head-shaking symptoms, read Why Does My Dog Shake His Head?.

Trusted reference

Pet owners can find general preventive-care information through the American Veterinary Medical Association pet-owner resources.

FAQ

Why does my dog lick only one paw?

A localized problem such as a foreign object, nail injury, sting, wound, or pain becomes more important to consider when only one paw is affected.

Why are my dog's paws red from licking?

Repeated licking can irritate skin, but redness may also be part of the original problem. Persistent redness needs veterinary assessment rather than simply stopping the licking.

Can boredom cause paw licking?

It can contribute in some dogs, but persistent licking should first be evaluated for medical causes.

Bottom line: Treat paw licking as information. Check the feet carefully, notice whether one or several paws are affected, and seek veterinary help when the behavior persists or there are signs of injury, infection, or pain.

title: Why Is My Dog Not Eating? Common Causes, Warning Signs and What to Do
summary: A dog skipping food can have many explanations. Learn how to assess appetite changes safely and which signs mean veterinary care should not wait.
primaryKeyword: why is my dog not eating
secondaryKeywords: when to call vet dog not eating
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog sitting beside a full food bowl while owner observes
content:
A sudden loss of appetite deserves attention because it is a change, not a diagnosis. Some dogs briefly eat less after stress or a routine change, but reduced appetite can also accompany dental pain, stomach upset, infection, medication effects, pain elsewhere in the body, or more serious illness.

First, define what “not eating” means

Did your dog refuse one meal, eat half the usual amount, reject kibble but accept treats, or stop eating entirely? Also note water intake, vomiting, diarrhea, energy level, urination, bowel movements, and any recent access to garbage, toys, bones, medications, or toxins. These details help determine urgency.

Common reasons appetite changes

Routine or environmental change

Travel, boarding, a new pet, a move, unusual noise, or a change in feeding schedule can affect some dogs. Appetite should still be monitored, especially if other symptoms appear.

Dental or mouth pain

A dog may approach food but hesitate, drop kibble, chew on one side, drool, or prefer softer food. Broken teeth, gum disease, oral injuries, and other painful conditions need veterinary assessment.

Digestive upset

Nausea, dietary indiscretion, abrupt food changes, intestinal disease, and other gastrointestinal problems can reduce appetite. Vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, or repeated attempts to vomit make the situation more concerning.

Pain or illness elsewhere

Dogs often eat less when they feel unwell. Because appetite loss is nonspecific, a physical examination may be needed to identify the cause.

What owners can do safely

  • Offer the dog's normal food at the normal time rather than cycling through many rich foods.
  • Keep fresh water available unless a veterinarian has instructed otherwise.
  • Record when the dog last ate a normal meal and how much has been eaten since.
  • Check for vomiting, diarrhea, bloating, pain, weakness, or unusual behavior.
  • Keep medications, trash, toxic foods, and foreign objects out of reach.

When not to wait

Contact a veterinarian promptly if your dog refuses food and is a puppy, very small dog, senior, pregnant, has a chronic condition, takes important medication, or has other symptoms. Urgent assessment is appropriate for repeated vomiting, a swollen or painful abdomen, unproductive retching, collapse, marked weakness, breathing difficulty, suspected toxin exposure, suspected foreign-body ingestion, blood in vomit or stool, or severe pain.

Do not force-feed

Force-feeding can be stressful and may be unsafe in a nauseated, weak, or neurologically impaired dog. Do not give human appetite stimulants or stomach medicines without veterinary direction.

Related Virixoo guides

If vomiting is part of the problem, read Why Is My Dog Vomiting?. For loose stool, see Why Does My Dog Have Diarrhea?.

Trusted reference

For reliable pet-owner health information, see the AVMA resources for pet owners.

FAQ

My dog is not eating but is drinking. Is that okay?

Drinking is useful information, but it does not rule out illness. Duration, age, medical history, and other symptoms matter.

Can I tempt my dog with human food?

Repeatedly offering rich foods can worsen digestive upset and obscure the appetite pattern. Ask your veterinarian what is appropriate if your dog is unwell.

How long can I wait?

There is no single safe waiting period for every dog. Young, old, medically fragile, or symptomatic dogs need earlier veterinary advice. If the appetite change is unusual for your dog or persists, call your veterinarian.

Bottom line: A missed meal can be minor, but appetite loss becomes more meaningful when it persists or appears with other symptoms. Observe the whole dog, not just the bowl.

title: Why Is My Dog Vomiting? What the Pattern Can Mean and When to Call a Vet
summary: Learn how to describe dog vomiting, what owners should monitor, safe immediate steps, and red flags that require prompt veterinary care.
secondaryKeywords: dog vomiting when to see vet
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Concerned owner comforting a dog near a clean floor after vomiting
content:
Vomiting is common enough that many owners see it at least once, but repeated or severe vomiting can become dangerous. The most useful first step is to distinguish an isolated episode in an otherwise normal dog from vomiting accompanied by pain, weakness, dehydration, toxin exposure, or other warning signs.

Vomiting versus regurgitation

Vomiting is an active process and may include nausea, drooling, abdominal contractions, or retching. Regurgitation is often more passive, with food or fluid coming back up without obvious abdominal effort. A short video, if safe to take, can help your veterinarian distinguish the two.

Possible reasons dogs vomit

Dogs can vomit after dietary indiscretion, sudden food changes, motion sickness, gastrointestinal inflammation, parasites, pancreatitis, foreign-body obstruction, toxin exposure, medication reactions, systemic illness, and many other conditions. Because the list is broad, the pattern and accompanying signs matter more than trying to diagnose the cause at home.

Information worth recording

ObservationWhy it helps
Number of episodesShows whether the problem is isolated or recurring
Food, foam, bile, blood, or foreign materialHelps characterize the episode
Water intakeHelps assess hydration and whether drinking triggers more vomiting
Stool changesVomiting plus diarrhea can change the clinical picture
Possible toxin or object accessMay make evaluation urgent

What to do after an isolated episode

Keep your dog calm and observe closely. Do not give human anti-nausea drugs or other medicines unless a veterinarian specifically recommends them. Because feeding and water advice can differ based on age, size, medical history, and the cause of vomiting, call your veterinary clinic for individualized guidance if vomiting continues.

Emergency warning signs

Seek urgent veterinary care for repeated unproductive retching, a swollen or painful abdomen, collapse, severe weakness, breathing difficulty, suspected poisoning, known or suspected foreign-object ingestion, significant blood, repeated vomiting that prevents water from staying down, or rapidly worsening condition. Puppies and medically fragile dogs can deteriorate more quickly and deserve a lower threshold for professional advice.

Related Virixoo guides

If appetite has also changed, read Why Is My Dog Not Eating?. If diarrhea is present, see Why Does My Dog Have Diarrhea?.

Trusted reference

For general veterinary information and help finding veterinary care, visit the American Animal Hospital Association.

FAQ

Is yellow vomit always serious?

Yellow fluid is often bile, but color alone cannot determine severity. Frequency, behavior, hydration, pain, and other symptoms are more important.

Should I give my dog a human stomach medicine?

No medicine should be given simply because it is available at home. Doses, contraindications, and the underlying cause matter; ask a veterinarian first.

Why does my dog vomit repeatedly after drinking?

Repeated inability to keep water down can lead to dehydration and may indicate a significant problem. Contact a veterinarian promptly.

Bottom line: One episode in a bright, comfortable dog is different from repeated vomiting in a painful or weak dog. Count episodes, note associated signs, and escalate quickly when red flags appear.

title: Why Does My Dog Have Diarrhea? Common Triggers and Safe Next Steps
summary: A practical guide to diarrhea in dogs, including common triggers, what to monitor, hydration concerns, and veterinary warning signs.
primaryKeyword: why does my dog have diarrhea
secondaryKeywords: dog diarrhea when to see vet
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog owner walking a dog outdoors while monitoring its health
content:
Loose stool can follow a simple dietary upset, but it can also be a sign of infection, parasites, inflammation, toxin exposure, or other illness. Instead of focusing only on stool consistency, assess how your dog feels overall.

Common triggers

Potential causes include sudden diet changes, eating garbage or unfamiliar foods, stress, intestinal parasites, infections, medication effects, food intolerance, inflammatory conditions, and systemic disease. Puppies, seniors, and dogs with chronic medical conditions may need veterinary advice sooner than a healthy adult.

What to monitor

  • How often your dog needs to defecate.
  • Whether stool is soft, watery, mucus-coated, black/tarry, or visibly bloody.
  • Vomiting, appetite, thirst, energy, and abdominal discomfort.
  • Possible access to garbage, spoiled food, toys, bones, chemicals, or medication.
  • Recent diet, boarding, travel, stress, or parasite-prevention changes.

Hydration matters

Diarrhea causes fluid loss. Keep fresh water available unless a veterinarian advises otherwise, and watch for worsening lethargy, dry or tacky gums, weakness, or reduced urination. Do not rely on a home dehydration test to rule out a problem.

Do not reach for human anti-diarrheal drugs

Some human medicines are inappropriate for certain dogs or may mask an important problem. Treatment depends on the cause, so medication should be discussed with a veterinarian.

When to call the vet

Contact a veterinarian when diarrhea is frequent, persists, repeatedly returns, or occurs with vomiting, poor appetite, pain, feverish behavior, weakness, dehydration, or weight loss. Seek prompt care for black/tarry stool, substantial blood, collapse, severe abdominal pain, suspected toxin exposure, or suspected foreign-object ingestion.

Should you bring a stool sample?

If your clinic requests one, a fresh sample in a clean, sealed container can be useful for testing. Ask the clinic how they want it stored and transported.

Related Virixoo guides

For vomiting at the same time, read Why Is My Dog Vomiting?. If your dog has stopped eating, see Why Is My Dog Not Eating?.

Trusted reference

The American Veterinary Medical Association provides pet-owner education and veterinary-care resources.

FAQ

Can stress cause diarrhea in dogs?

Stress can contribute to gastrointestinal signs in some dogs, but persistent or severe diarrhea should not automatically be attributed to stress.

Is blood in diarrhea an emergency?

Small streaks and large amounts of blood do not have the same implications, but blood warrants veterinary advice. Black, tarry stool or substantial bleeding requires prompt assessment.

Should I switch foods immediately?

Repeated food changes can worsen digestive upset. Ask your veterinarian about the best feeding plan if diarrhea persists.

Bottom line: The urgency of diarrhea depends on the dog, duration, frequency, and accompanying signs. Monitor hydration and behavior closely and seek professional care when the problem is persistent, severe, or accompanied by red flags.

title: How to Help a Dog With Separation Anxiety: A Gradual, Low-Stress Plan
summary: Learn the signs of separation-related distress and a humane, gradual plan that avoids punishment and overwhelming absences.
primaryKeyword: how to help a dog with separation anxiety
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Calm dog resting near the front door with an enrichment toy
content:
A dog who panics when left alone is not being spiteful. Separation-related distress can involve barking, howling, pacing, drooling, house soiling, destruction near exits, or escape attempts. The goal is not to punish the behavior; it is to reduce the dog's distress and build tolerance to being alone at a pace the dog can handle.

First, make sure the pattern fits

Use a pet camera if possible. Note what happens before departure, how quickly signs begin after you leave, and whether the same behaviors occur while you are home. Medical problems and other behavior issues can resemble separation anxiety, so a veterinarian is an important starting point for severe or sudden cases.

Step 1: identify your dog's threshold

The threshold is roughly how long your dog can remain comfortable before distress begins. For some dogs it may be minutes; for severe cases it may be seconds. Training that repeatedly pushes far beyond that point can make practice less useful.

Step 2: practice very short absences

Start below the threshold. Perform a normal departure, leave briefly, and return while the dog is still calm. Over many sessions, duration can be increased gradually. Progress is rarely perfectly linear; shorten the next session if the dog shows escalating distress.

Step 3: reduce the power of departure cues

Keys, shoes, bags, and coats can predict a long absence. At calm times, occasionally pick up keys or put on shoes without leaving so these cues become less reliable predictors. Do not deliberately tease or repeatedly agitate the dog.

Step 4: build a comfortable routine

Appropriate exercise, sniffing walks, food puzzles, chewing opportunities, and predictable rest can support overall wellbeing. Enrichment is useful, but a dog in true panic may ignore food; refusing a normally valuable food toy on departure can itself be useful information.

What not to do

  • Do not punish destruction, barking, or accidents after you return.
  • Do not use “cry it out” as a default strategy for a dog showing panic.
  • Do not assume another dog will automatically solve the problem.
  • Do not confine a dog in a crate if confinement triggers frantic escape attempts or self-injury.

When professional help is appropriate

Contact your veterinarian if distress is intense, the dog injures itself, cannot tolerate even brief absences, or the problem appeared suddenly. A veterinarian can assess medical contributors and discuss whether referral to a veterinary behaviorist or other qualified behavior professional is appropriate. Medication can be part of treatment for some dogs and should be prescribed and monitored professionally.

A realistic progress table

Dog's responseTraining decision
Relaxed, takes food, settlesRepeat or make the next absence slightly longer
Alert but recovers quicklyKeep duration similar until consistently comfortable
Pacing, vocalizing, panting, escape behaviorShorten the next practice and seek help if severe

Related Virixoo guides

For general barking, read Why Does My Dog Bark So Much?. For calm leash-based enrichment outside the home, see How to Stop a Dog From Pulling on the Leash.

Trusted references

Read the ASPCA separation anxiety guide and the AAHA overview of separation anxiety in pets.

FAQ

Should I ignore my dog before leaving?

Calm, predictable departures are generally preferable to dramatic ones, but treatment should focus on the dog's emotional response and gradual alone-time training rather than rigid rituals.

Will a crate fix separation anxiety?

Not by itself. A crate can be comfortable for some trained dogs, but it can worsen distress in dogs who panic when confined.

How fast should I increase alone time?

There is no universal schedule. Increase only while your dog remains comfortable; severe cases often benefit from professional guidance.

Bottom line: Separation anxiety is a welfare issue, not a discipline problem. Observe the dog, work below the panic threshold, progress gradually, and involve veterinary or behavior professionals when distress is significant.

title: How to Stop a Dog From Pulling on the Leash: A Reward-Based Walking Plan
summary: Teach loose-leash walking with clear rewards, manageable practice sessions, and equipment choices that prioritize comfort and safety.
primaryKeyword: how to stop dog pulling on leash
secondaryKeywords: teach dog to walk beside me
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog walking calmly on a loose leash beside its owner
content:
Dogs pull because moving forward is rewarding. If a tight leash repeatedly gets a dog to the tree, smell, person, or park entrance it wants, pulling is reinforced. Loose-leash training changes that pattern by making slack in the leash the reliable way to keep the walk moving.

Choose practical equipment

Use a secure, well-fitted collar or harness and a standard leash appropriate for your dog's size. Check fit before each walk. Dogs with respiratory, orthopedic, or neck concerns may need individualized equipment advice from a veterinarian. Avoid equipment that causes pain or relies on intimidation.

Teach the skill somewhere easy first

A busy sidewalk is a difficult classroom. Begin indoors, in a hallway, yard, or quiet area. Reward your dog for being near you with a loose leash. Take a few steps, reward again, then gradually increase the number of steps between rewards.

What to do when the leash becomes tight

Stop forward progress rather than dragging the dog back. When the dog turns toward you or creates slack, mark or praise that choice and move again. Another option is a calm change of direction. Consistency matters more than strength.

Use the environment as a reward

Food is useful, but sniffing is valuable too. Ask for several loose-leash steps, then release your dog to sniff an appropriate area. This teaches that cooperation does not end the fun; it helps the dog access it.

Keep sessions short enough to succeed

Five focused minutes can teach more than a long frustrating walk. For energetic dogs, separate exercise needs from training when possible: provide suitable play or enrichment so every walk is not carrying the full burden of physical activity.

Common mistakes

  • Allowing pulling sometimes and stopping it only when convenient.
  • Expecting heel position for an entire recreational walk.
  • Starting in environments that are too distracting.
  • Holding the leash constantly tight.
  • Punishing the dog for noticing normal sights and smells.

If your dog lunges or reacts

Pulling toward smells is different from barking, lunging, freezing, or showing fear/aggression toward dogs or people. Increase distance from triggers and seek qualified professional help if safety is a concern. Do not force close encounters.

Related Virixoo guides

Dogs that become highly aroused outside may also benefit from Why Does My Dog Bark So Much?. If alone-time distress is part of the bigger picture, see How to Help a Dog With Separation Anxiety.

Trusted reference

For professional behavior resources and humane behavior guidance, visit the ASPCA behavioral help resource.

FAQ

Should my dog walk at my heel all the time?

No. A formal heel is useful in some situations, but recreational walks can allow safe sniffing and exploration while maintaining a loose leash.

Why does my dog pull more near home?

Anticipation, familiar smells, routine, and learned reinforcement can all affect pulling. Practice in easier locations and reward slack before the dog reaches peak excitement.

How long does leash training take?

It varies with the dog's learning history, environment, consistency, and arousal level. Measure progress by more frequent loose-leash moments rather than expecting an instant cure.

Bottom line: Loose-leash walking is a trained skill. Make slack rewarding, stop letting pulling reliably move the dog forward, and practice where your dog can succeed.

title: How to Stop Puppy Biting: What Is Normal and How to Teach a Softer Mouth
summary: Puppy mouthing is normal, but owners can teach safer play through redirection, short breaks, appropriate chew outlets, and consistent handling.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Playful puppy holding a soft toy instead of mouthing hands
content:
Puppies explore with their mouths. Mouthing, chewing, and nipping are common during play and development, but that does not mean owners should simply tolerate painful biting. The goal is to teach the puppy what to bite, how to calm down, and that hard contact with human skin ends the interaction.

Why puppies bite

Common reasons include play, exploration, teething, excitement, fatigue, frustration, and seeking interaction. Context matters. A loose, wiggly puppy grabbing sleeves during play looks different from a stiff puppy growling or biting when approached near food or when handled.

Redirect before the bite

Keep appropriate toys within reach. If the puppy targets hands, clothing, or ankles, present a toy and reward engagement with it. Use non-contact games such as fetch and structured tug rather than encouraging wrestling with hands.

Use brief, calm breaks

If biting becomes too hard or persistent, calmly stop interaction for a short period. The lesson is simple: gentle play continues; painful biting makes the fun pause. Avoid yelling, hitting, muzzle-grabbing, or other physical punishment, which can increase fear or arousal.

Watch for the overtired puppy

Many puppies become especially mouthy when they need sleep. Puppies require substantial rest. A predictable routine with naps, meals, toilet trips, play, short training sessions, and quiet chewing opportunities can reduce chaotic over-arousal.

Provide legal chewing outlets

Offer puppy-safe chew items appropriate for your dog's size and chewing style, and supervise until you know how the puppy uses them. Replace damaged toys that could break into swallowable pieces. Ask your veterinarian about suitable options if you are unsure.

Teach useful alternatives

Reward simple behaviors such as sit, touch, looking at you, or picking up a toy. These give the puppy something specific to do when excitement rises. Training sessions should be short and rewarding.

When biting needs professional attention

Seek help if biting is accompanied by repeated stiffening, guarding, intense fear, sustained growling, bites that cause significant injury, or unpredictable aggression. Pain can also change behavior, so sudden biting in a previously tolerant puppy deserves veterinary assessment.

Children and puppies

Active supervision is essential. Children should not be expected to manage puppy biting themselves. Use gates or pens to create separation when adults cannot actively supervise, and teach children not to hug, corner, chase, or disturb a sleeping or eating puppy.

Related Virixoo guides

As your puppy learns outside skills, continue with How to Stop a Dog From Pulling on the Leash. For barking and over-arousal, see Why Does My Dog Bark So Much?.

Trusted reference

The ASPCA guide to puppy mouthing, nipping and biting explains normal mouthing and humane training approaches.

FAQ

Will my puppy simply grow out of biting?

Mouthing often decreases with maturity, but puppies still benefit from being taught appropriate play and bite inhibition.

Should I yelp when my puppy bites?

Some puppies pause when they hear a yelp; others become more excited. If it increases arousal, skip it and use calm withdrawal and redirection instead.

Is teething the only reason puppies bite?

No. Teething contributes, but play, excitement, fatigue, frustration, and exploration are also common.

Bottom line: Puppy biting is best handled with prevention, redirection, short consequences, enough rest, and safe chewing—not fear or physical punishment.

title: Why Does My Dog Bark So Much? Find the Trigger Before You Try to Stop It
summary: Excessive barking has different causes. Learn how to identify the trigger, reduce rehearsal, reward quiet alternatives, and know when professional help is needed.
primaryKeyword: why does my dog bark so much
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Alert dog looking through a window while owner redirects attention
content:
Barking is communication, not a single behavior with a single solution. Dogs bark for alerting, excitement, fear, frustration, attention, play, territorial responses, and separation-related distress. Effective training starts by identifying what happens immediately before and after the barking.

Keep a barking log for several days

RecordExample
TriggerPerson passes the window
Distance/intensityAcross street vs at front door
What dog doesBarks, runs to window, stiffens
What happens nextPerson leaves, owner shouts

This can reveal patterns that are easy to miss in the moment.

Alert barking at windows

Reduce rehearsal by limiting access to the visual trigger when you cannot train. During planned practice, reward the dog for noticing a low-intensity trigger and turning back to you. Increase distance or reduce intensity if the dog cannot disengage.

Attention barking

If barking reliably produces play, food, door opening, or eye contact, it can become an efficient strategy. Meet legitimate needs proactively, then reward an alternative such as sitting quietly or going to a mat. Avoid accidentally creating long barking contests.

Fear or reactivity

A dog barking with a tense body, retreating, lunging, or showing other signs of fear needs more than a “quiet” cue. Create distance, prevent forced greetings, and consider professional behavior help. Punishing warning behavior can suppress communication without resolving the underlying emotion.

Barking when alone

If barking begins soon after departure and occurs with pacing, drooling, destruction, house soiling, or escape behavior, investigate separation-related distress rather than treating it as ordinary nuisance barking.

Meet normal needs

Age-appropriate exercise, sniffing, social interaction, rest, training, and enrichment can reduce barking that is amplified by unmet needs. More exercise is not a cure for every barking problem, however; frightened or anxious dogs need an emotion-focused plan.

When to involve your veterinarian

Sudden behavior change, barking associated with pain, confusion in an older dog, or severe anxiety warrants veterinary assessment. A qualified behavior professional can help when barking involves aggression, intense fear, or major household disruption.

Related Virixoo guides

If barking occurs primarily during absences, read How to Help a Dog With Separation Anxiety. For outdoor pulling and arousal, see How to Stop a Dog From Pulling on the Leash.

Trusted reference

The ASPCA dog behavior resource explains that different types of barking and other behavior problems require cause-specific approaches.

FAQ

Should I teach a “quiet” cue?

It can be useful, but it works best alongside trigger management and reinforcement of calm behavior rather than as the only strategy.

Why does yelling not work?

Yelling may add excitement or attention and does not teach the dog what to do instead. It also does not address fear or anxiety.

Can I stop all barking?

That is neither realistic nor desirable. The goal is usually to reduce excessive barking and improve the dog's ability to respond calmly.

Bottom line: Before trying to stop barking, determine its function. Change the environment, teach an alternative, and address fear or anxiety rather than punishing the sound.

title: Why Does My Dog Shake His Head? Ear Problems, Irritation and Warning Signs
summary: Occasional head shaking is normal, but repeated shaking can signal ear irritation, infection, allergy, a foreign object, or pain. Learn what to check safely.
primaryKeyword: why does my dog shake his head
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog tilting its head while owner gently looks at the outer ear
content:
A single head shake after waking or getting wet is usually ordinary; repeated head shaking deserves a closer look. Dogs shake their heads when something in or around the ear feels itchy, wet, painful, or irritating.

Common possibilities

Ear inflammation or infection

Redness, odor, discharge, tenderness, or repeated ear scratching can accompany ear disease. Bacteria and yeast may be involved, but treatment depends on what is happening inside the ear and whether the eardrum is healthy.

Allergy

Recurring ear problems can occur alongside allergic skin disease. Paw licking, generalized itching, or seasonal flare-ups are useful details to tell your veterinarian.

Water or debris

Head shaking may start after bathing or swimming. Grass material and other foreign objects can also enter the ear canal, sometimes causing sudden intense shaking on one side.

Ear mites or other parasites

Parasites are possible, particularly in certain environments and animals, but dark debris alone cannot confirm the cause. A veterinary ear examination and microscopic testing may be needed.

What you can check safely

Look only at the visible outer ear. Compare both sides for redness, swelling, odor, discharge, wounds, or obvious debris. Stop if touching the ear causes pain or defensive behavior.

What not to put in the ear

Do not insert cotton swabs deep into the canal. Avoid peroxide, alcohol, essential oils, leftover ear medications, or unprescribed cleaners in a painful ear. Some products can irritate tissue, and certain medications may be unsafe if the eardrum is damaged.

Why repeated shaking should not be ignored

Strong, repeated shaking can traumatize the ear flap and contribute to an aural hematoma, a swollen pocket of blood in the pinna. Treating the underlying ear problem early can reduce ongoing discomfort and self-trauma.

When to call the veterinarian

Arrange veterinary care for persistent shaking, pain, odor, discharge, marked redness, swelling, head tilt, balance problems, or recurrent ear trouble. Sudden severe neurologic signs, inability to stand normally, or significant trauma require prompt care.

Related Virixoo guides

If ear trouble occurs with itchy skin, read Why Is My Dog Scratching So Much?. If your dog also chews its feet, see Why Does My Dog Lick His Paws?.

Trusted reference

For preventive veterinary guidance and information on accredited animal hospitals, visit AAHA.

FAQ

Can I clean my dog's ear at home?

Routine cleaning can be appropriate for some dogs, but a painful, inflamed, or suddenly symptomatic ear should be assessed before you add products.

Why is only one ear affected?

A one-sided problem can occur with infection, debris, a foreign object, trauma, or other localized causes. Sudden intense one-sided shaking is worth prompt veterinary advice.

Can allergies cause ear infections?

Allergic skin disease can contribute to recurring ear inflammation in some dogs, but a veterinarian should evaluate recurrent cases rather than assuming allergy is the only cause.

Bottom line: Repeated head shaking is a sign of discomfort. Inspect only what you can see safely, avoid home remedies inside a painful ear, and get veterinary help when the behavior persists or other ear signs appear.
